\chapter{School: The Borrowed Word and the Built One}
\label{ch:hi-skool-vidyalaya}
\hlchaptermodality{89}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the school in both registers, say who is in it, and tell which of the two words belongs on a sign and which in a spoken sentence.}

Say where the teacher and the student are using the casual word, then read the sign that calls the same building by the formal one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[skūl]{\hi{स्कूल} (skūl) — the building the teacher and the student were always in}

\label{lesson:HI-C81-skool}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\hi{शिक्षक}} and \emph{chātra}. You have had both of them for a long time. Now say the place they meet — and notice that you cannot yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{स्कूल}}
\textbf{\hi{स्कूल}} (\emph{skūl}) — \textquotedblleft{}school\textquotedblright{}. Masculine.

Write it: \hi{स} + \hi{्} + \hi{क} gives the conjunct \textbf{\hi{स्क}}, then \hi{ू} above the \hi{ल}... no: the \hi{ू} belongs to \hi{क}, so it is \textbf{\hi{स्कू}} and then \textbf{\hi{ल}}. Three pieces, one of them a conjunct you have seen before.

\begin{cousinweb}
This one is borrowed straight from English, and the English word has a joke inside it that Hindi inherited without asking.

English \emph{school} comes from Latin \emph{schola}, from Greek \textbf{skhol\'{\={e}}} — which meant \textbf{leisure}. Free time. The hours you did not have to work.

The Greeks thought study was what a person did with their leisure, so the word for time off slid across to mean the place you spend it learning. Every language that borrowed it borrowed the joke: Spanish \emph{escuela}, German \emph{Schule}, Russian \emph{shkola}, and now Hindi \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}}.

So when you say \emph{skūl}, you are saying a Greek word for \textquotedblleft{}spare time\textquotedblright{} that has travelled through Latin, English and into Devanagari without anyone noticing what it used to mean.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{स्कूल}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{skūl}
  \item the teacher, the student, and the school, in that order (\hi{शिक्षक}, \emph{chātra}, \hi{स्कूल})
  \item what the Greek ancestor of this word meant (leisure)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{skhol\'{\={e}}} mean before it meant school? (Leisure — the time you did not have to work.) Which two people did this track already know how to name before it could name the building? (\hi{शिक्षक} and \emph{chātra}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vidyālay]{\hi{विद्यालय} (vidyālay) — an abode of knowledge}

\label{lesson:HI-C81-vidyalaya}



\begin{quote}
You have \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}}, borrowed whole. Hindi also has its own word, built out of two pieces you can take apart. Guess which register it belongs to before reading on — the sign above the gate, or the sentence a child says?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{विद्यालय}}
\textbf{\hi{विद्यालय}} (\emph{vidyālay}) — \textquotedblleft{}school\textquotedblright{}, masculine, and noticeably more formal than \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}}. It is what you read on the gate, on a form, in a newspaper. A child telling you where they are going says \emph{skūl}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Two Sanskrit pieces, joined the way Sanskrit joins everything:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{विद्या}} (\emph{vidyā}) — \textquotedblleft{}knowledge\textquotedblright{} — plus \textbf{\hi{आलय}} (\emph{ālaya}) — \textquotedblleft{}abode\textquotedblright{}. An abode of knowledge.
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{आलय}} is productive on its own: \emph{himālaya} is \textbf{\hi{हिम}} (\textquotedblleft{}snow\textquotedblright{}) + \hi{आलय} — the abode of snow. You already know that mountain's name; now you know it is a compound, and the second half is sitting in this word too.

And \textbf{\hi{विद्या}} rests on the root \textbf{\hi{विद्}} (\emph{vid}), \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{} — which is one of the furthest-travelled roots in any language on earth:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{वेद}} (\emph{veda}) — knowledge, the name of the oldest texts.
  \item Latin \emph{vidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}, giving \textbf{vid}eo, \textbf{vis}ion, e\textbf{vid}ence.
  \item English \textbf{wit}, \textbf{wis}dom, and the \emph{-wise} in \emph{likewise}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{vidyālay} and the English word \emph{wit} are built on the same ancient syllable. The borrowed \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}} carried a Greek word for leisure into Hindi; the native \textbf{\hi{विद्यालय}} was here all along, and its root reaches English by a different road entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{विद्यालय}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vidyālay}
  \item which of the two words goes on the gate and which a child says
  \item the other famous compound ending in \hi{आलय}, and what its first half means (\hi{हिमालय} — \hi{हिम}, snow)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \textbf{\hi{विद्यालय}}? (\hi{विद्या} knowledge + \hi{आलय} abode.) Which English word for cleverness comes from the same root as \hi{विद्या}? (\emph{Wit} — and \emph{wisdom} with it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[skūl / vidyālay]{\hi{स्कूल} or \hi{विद्यालय} — the same building, two registers}

\label{lesson:HI-C81-repaso-skool}



\begin{quote}
Both words mean school. Say each one, and decide which you would write on an official form.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: borrowed whole, or built from parts}]
This is the third time this pattern has turned up, and it is worth naming:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{borrowed whole} & \textbf{built from parts} \\
\midrule
a meal & \hi{नाश्ता} & \hi{दोपहर} \hi{का} \hi{खाना} \\
a school & \hi{स्कूल} & \hi{विद्यालय} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Hindi keeps both kinds and uses them at different heights. The borrowed word is what people say; the built word is what institutions write. Neither is more correct, and a learner who only has one of them will sound wrong in half the situations they meet.

Note which way round it falls here: the \textbf{borrowed} word is the casual one. That is not a rule — it is what happened to these two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the casual word, then the formal one
  \item the student, and where the student goes, casually (\emph{chātra}, \hi{स्कूल})
  \item what \hi{विद्यालय} is made of, in two pieces
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two would appear on a gate, and which in a child's sentence? (\hi{विद्यालय} on the gate, \hi{स्कूल} in the sentence.) Which other pair in this book splits the same way? (\hi{नाश्ता} and \hi{दोपहर} \hi{का} \hi{खाना}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śikṣak skūl meṁ haiṁ]{\hi{शिक्षक} \hi{स्कूल} \hi{में} \hi{हैं} — the building, with people in it}

\label{lesson:HI-C81-sintesis-skool}



\begin{quote}
A place you can name is not yet a place you can put somebody in. Say where the teacher is, out loud, before reading on.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Every word here is one you have met:

\begin{quote}
\hi{शिक्षक} \hi{स्कूल} \hi{में} \hi{हैं।} \emph{chātra} \hi{भी} \hi{स्कूल} \hi{में} \hi{हैं।} \hi{विद्यालय} \hi{बड़ा} \hi{है।}
\end{quote}

Three short lines, and the third one changes register on purpose: the sign over the door calls the building \textbf{\hi{विद्यालय}}, even though the two sentences before it called the same building \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the reading paper cares}]
This matters beyond the vocabulary. An exam reading paper is built out of signs, forms and notices — exactly the places where the \textbf{formal} word appears — while the listening paper is built out of people talking, where the \textbf{casual} word does.

A candidate who knows only \textbf{\hi{स्कूल}} can follow the conversation and stall on the sign. A candidate who knows only \textbf{\hi{विद्यालय}} does the reverse.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{शिक्षक} \hi{स्कूल} \hi{में} \hi{हैं।}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same sentence about the student (\emph{chātra})
  \item the third line, with the formal word (\hi{विद्यालय} \hi{बड़ा} \hi{है।})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two school words would you expect on a sign in a reading paper, and which in a spoken exchange? (\hi{विद्यालय} on the sign, \hi{स्कूल} in the exchange.) Say where the student is.
\end{tcolorbox}
